title: Fakes and Replay: Testing Code That Talks to Hardware

questions.question: Why can code that names a concrete device not be tested properly?
options: Because devices are too slow for tests
Because device drivers are always written in C
Because hardware access requires administrator permissions
It only runs where that device is, and the device will not fail on demand
questions.explanation: Three problems at once: nobody without the device can run it, the readings are never repeatable, and the interesting failures happen on the device's schedule rather than yours.

questions.question: What is the difference between a fake and a mock?
options: A fake is for hardware, a mock is for software
There is no difference
A fake is a working implementation with a shortcut, a mock records how it was called
A mock is faster than a fake
questions.explanation: Fakes make tests read like descriptions of behaviour. Mock heavy suites describe implementation, and break when the implementation changes even though the behaviour did not.

questions.question: Why does SensorSource need a virtual destructor?
options: To allow the class to be copied
Deleting a derived object through a base pointer without one is undefined behaviour
Because it has pure virtual functions
Because unique_ptr requires it
questions.explanation: The derived part is never destroyed, so anything it owns leaks quietly. It is the most common mistake with an interface.

questions.question: Why does the monitor count consecutive failures separately from total failures?
options: A sensor that drops one reading an hour is healthy, one that drops five in a row is not
So the mean can be corrected afterwards
Because the total is expensive to compute
Because consecutive failures are more accurate
questions.explanation: Treating every dropout as a fault produces a robot that stops constantly. The run length is what distinguishes noise from a device that has actually gone.

questions.question: What is the value of replaying a recorded trace rather than generating values?
options: It removes the need for an interface
It guarantees the code works on hardware
Every test afterwards is a reproduction of something a real device actually did
It runs faster than generating numbers
questions.explanation: Recorded data carries the oddities real devices produce and invented data does not. It also turns needing a LiDAR into needing a file.

questions.question: A test passes with the fake and fails on real hardware. What is the most likely reason?
options: The interface is wrong
The fake is more cooperative than the device: never late, never out of range, never gone mid read
The hardware is faulty
The test was written incorrectly
questions.explanation: A fake only exhibits what it was told to. Every difference you discover on hardware is worth adding to the fake so it is covered from then on.
